     1	# frozen_string_literal: true
     2	
     3	module WovenMonopoly
     4	  # A square on the board. Each kind of space decides for itself what happens
     5	  # when a player lands on it, so a new kind of space (jail, tax, chance...) is
     6	  # a new subclass plus one line in Board::SPACE_TYPES.
     7	  class Space
     8	    attr_reader :name
     9	
    10	    def initialize(name:)
    11	      @name = name
    12	    end
    13	
    14	    # Hook called by the game after a player has finished moving onto the space.
    15	    def land(_game, _player); end
    16	
    17	    # Builds a space from its JSON hash. Subclasses extend this with their own
    18	    # required keys.
    19	    def self.build(attrs)
    20	      new(name: fetch!(attrs, 'name', String))
    21	    end
    22	
    23	    def self.fetch!(attrs, key, klass)
    24	      value = attrs[key]
    25	      return value if value.is_a?(klass)
    26	
    27	      raise InvalidBoardError,
    28	            "space #{attrs['name'].inspect}: '#{key}' must be a #{klass.name.downcase}, got #{value.inspect}"
    29	    end
    30	  end
    31	
    32	  # The starting square. Passing it is handled by the board and the game, so
    33	  # landing on it does nothing extra.
    34	  class GoSpace < Space; end
    35	
    36	  # A square that must be bought when unowned and that charges rent when owned.
    37	  class PropertySpace < Space
    38	    attr_reader :price, :colour
    39	
    40	    def initialize(name:, price:, colour:)
    41	      super(name: name)
    42	      @price = price
    43	      @colour = colour
    44	    end
    45	
    46	    def self.build(attrs)
    47	      price = fetch!(attrs, 'price', Integer)
    48	      raise InvalidBoardError, "space #{attrs['name'].inspect}: price must be positive" unless price.positive?
    49	
    50	      new(name: fetch!(attrs, 'name', String), price: price, colour: fetch!(attrs, 'colour', String))
    51	    end
    52	
    53	    def land(game, player)
    54	      owner = game.owner_of(self)
    55	      if owner.nil?
    56	        game.buy(player, self)
    57	      elsif owner != player
    58	        game.charge_rent(player, owner, self)
    59	      end
    60	    end
    61	  end
    62	end

# Woven Monopoly: the architecture and every file explained

Your brief is in `data/TASK_BRIEF.md`. I'll explain the code in the order it runs, then the tests, then how to prepare for the interview. That matters because part of the interview is done without AI.

---

## 1. The big picture

The program reads a board and a list of dice rolls, plays the game until someone goes bankrupt or the rolls run out, and prints the result.

```
bin/woven_monopoly  ──►  CLI  ──►  Board.from_file(board.json)  ──►  [GoSpace, PropertySpace, ...]
   (entry point)          │        load_rolls(rolls.json)       ──►  [1, 3, 1, ...]
                          ▼
                        Game.new(board:, rolls:, rules: Rules.new)
                          │  play: for each roll →
                          │    1. Board#advance   (move, count GO passes)
                          │    2. Player#receive  (GO bonus)
                          │    3. Space#land      (buy / pay rent)
                          ▼
                        Result  ──►  to_h (for --json)  or  summary (plain text)
```

The main design idea is that **each class has one job**. When a rule changes, ideally only one file changes. The brief says "Extensibility, since the rules will change", so expect the interview to test this.

| File | Purpose | Knows about |
|---|---|---|
| [bin/woven_monopoly](bin/woven_monopoly) | The script you run | CLI |
| [lib/woven_monopoly.rb](lib/woven_monopoly.rb) | Loads all the other files | everything |
| [errors.rb](lib/woven_monopoly/errors.rb) | Custom error types | nothing |
| [space.rb](lib/woven_monopoly/space.rb) | One square, and what happens when you land on it | Game's services |
| [board.rb](lib/woven_monopoly/board.rb) | Order of the squares, wrapping, passing GO | Spaces only (no money, no players) |
| [player.rb](lib/woven_monopoly/player.rb) | Name, money, position, bankrupt flag | nothing |
| [rules.rb](lib/woven_monopoly/rules.rb) | Fixed numbers and policies ($16, $1 GO bonus, rent formula) | nothing |
| [game.rb](lib/woven_monopoly/game.rb) | The turn loop and who owns what | all of the above |
| [result.rb](lib/woven_monopoly/result.rb) | Final state as data, plus its JSON and text forms | nothing |
| [cli.rb](lib/woven_monopoly/cli.rb) | Reads arguments, loads files, prints output | Game, Board, Result |

---

## 2. Ruby syntax you'll see everywhere

| Syntax | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `# frozen_string_literal: true` | The magic comment at the top of every file. String literals can't be changed in place, which is faster and safer. Convention, not logic. |
| `module WovenMonopoly ... end` | A namespace, so `Board` doesn't clash with another `Board`. Outside it you write `WovenMonopoly::Board`. |
| `@money` | An instance variable, one per object. Like `this.money` in Java/JS. |
| `attr_reader :name` | Generates a getter: `def name; @name; end` |
| `attr_accessor :position` | Getter and setter (`player.position = 3`) |
| `def self.build(...)` | A class method, called on the class: `Space.build(...)`. Like `static` in Java. |
| `def initialize(name:, money:)` | Constructor with **keyword arguments**, called as `Player.new(name: 'Ann', money: 16)` |
| `def bankrupt?` | A `?` suffix marks a method that returns true/false (convention) |
| `def fetch!` | A `!` suffix means "be careful": here it raises an error instead of returning nil |
| `x if condition` / `raise ... unless ok` | Modifier `if`/`unless` at the end of a line |
| `players.map(&:name)` | Shorthand for `players.map { \|p\| p.name }` |
| `foo&.name` | Safe navigation: returns nil instead of crashing when `foo` is nil |
| `%w[Peter Billy]` | `['Peter', 'Billy']` |
| `.freeze` | Makes an object immutable |
| Last expression | Ruby returns the last expression of a method automatically, so `return` is rarely needed |

---

## 3. File by file

### `bin/woven_monopoly` (entry point)

```ruby
#!/usr/bin/env ruby
require_relative '../lib/woven_monopoly'
exit WovenMonopoly::CLI.run(ARGV)
```
- `#!/usr/bin/env ruby` (the shebang) tells Mac/Linux to run this file with Ruby. **Windows ignores it**, so on your machine you run `ruby bin/woven_monopoly ...`.
- `ARGV` is the list of command-line arguments.
- `CLI.run` returns a number (0, 1 or 2), and `exit` turns it into the process exit code. Keeping `exit` out of `CLI` makes `CLI` testable, because calling `exit` inside a test would kill the test run.

### `lib/woven_monopoly.rb` (loader)

It just `require_relative`s every file. **Order matters**: `space` loads before `board` because `Board::SPACE_TYPES` refers to `GoSpace` and `PropertySpace` when the file loads.

### `errors.rb`

```ruby
class Error < StandardError; end
class InvalidBoardError < Error; end
class InvalidRollsError < Error; end
```
`<` means "inherits from". Because both specific errors inherit from `WovenMonopoly::Error`, the CLI can catch all of them with one `rescue Error`. Inheriting from `StandardError` (not `Exception`) is the Ruby convention for errors an application should handle.

### `space.rb` (the most important design idea)

```ruby
class Space
  def land(_game, _player); end          # default: do nothing
end

class GoSpace < Space; end               # inherits "do nothing"

class PropertySpace < Space
  def land(game, player)
    owner = game.owner_of(self)
    if owner.nil?
      game.buy(player, self)               # rule: must buy
    elsif owner != player
      game.charge_rent(player, owner, self) # rule: pay rent
    end                                    # own property: nothing (assumption 10)
  end
end
```
- This is **polymorphism**. The game loop calls `space.land(game, player)` without checking what kind of square it is, and each subclass decides what happens. Adding a Tax square means a new class and one line in `Board::SPACE_TYPES`, and **the game loop doesn't change**.
- `_game`: a leading underscore marks a parameter as deliberately unused.
- `super(name: name)` in `PropertySpace#initialize` calls the parent constructor.
- **`self.build(attrs)`** turns a JSON hash like `{"name"=>"Massizim","price"=>4,...}` into an object. `PropertySpace` overrides it to also read `price` and `colour`.
- **`fetch!(attrs, key, klass)`** is a validation helper. `value.is_a?(Integer)` checks the type. Because it's defined on `Space`, subclasses inherit it, so `PropertySpace.build` can call it.

### `board.rb` (layout only)

```ruby
SPACE_TYPES = { 'go' => GoSpace, 'property' => PropertySpace }.freeze
```
A **registry**: a hash from the JSON `"type"` string to a class. In Ruby, classes are ordinary objects, so you can keep them in a hash and call `.build` on whichever one you look up.

**How loading works.** Each method narrows the input and hands it to the next:
- `from_file(path)` reads the file. It turns `Errno::ENOENT` (file not found) into a friendly `InvalidBoardError`.
- `from_json(text)` runs `JSON.parse` and checks the result is an Array.
- `from_array(data)` builds every space with `data.map { |attrs| build_space(attrs) }`.
- `build_space` looks up the class in `SPACE_TYPES` and calls `klass.build(attrs)`.

Note the **method-level `rescue`**: in Ruby, a `def` body can end with a `rescue` clause without writing `begin`.

```ruby
def initialize(spaces)
  go_indexes = @spaces.each_index.select { |i| @spaces[i].is_a?(GoSpace) }
  raise InvalidBoardError, "...exactly one GO..." unless go_indexes.size == 1
```
GO is *found* on the board rather than assumed to be at index 0. That covers the brief's "boards can be different".

- `def [](index)` defines the `[]` operator, so you can write `board[3]`. `fetch` raises an error on a bad index, where `[]` would return nil.
- `colour_group(colour)` returns every property of that colour, so groups can be any size.

**`advance` (the trickiest method; be ready to explain it without AI):**
```ruby
def advance(from, steps)
  to = (from + steps) % size                       # wrap around
  distance_to_go = (@go_index - from) % size       # steps until next GO
  distance_to_go = size if distance_to_go.zero?    # standing ON GO → next GO is a full lap away
  passes = steps >= distance_to_go ? 1 + ((steps - distance_to_go) / size) : 0
  [to, passes]                                     # returns two values as an array
end
```
Worked example on the 9-square board, from Massizim (8), rolling 3:
- `to = 11 % 9 = 2` (Fast Kebabs)
- `distance_to_go = (0 - 8) % 9 = 1`. In Ruby, `%` with a positive divisor never returns a negative number. (In JavaScript, `-8 % 9` is `-8`.)
- `3 >= 1`, so `passes = 1 + (2 / 9) = 1 + 0 = 1`. Integer division truncates.

This is a "closed-form" formula: it computes the answer directly instead of stepping one square at a time, so a roll of 100 costs the same as a roll of 1.

### `player.rb`

```ruby
def pay(amount)
  paid = [amount, @money].min      # can't pay more than you have
  @money -= paid
  @bankrupt = true if paid < amount
  paid                              # return what was actually paid
end
```
Returning `paid` lets the caller credit the owner the right amount (assumption 6). Paying exactly all your money gives `paid == amount`, which is **not** bankrupt (assumption 7).

`money` has only an `attr_reader`, so nothing outside the class can set it directly. All changes go through `pay` and `receive`. That's **encapsulation**.

### `rules.rb`

```ruby
def initialize(player_names: DEFAULT_PLAYER_NAMES, starting_money: 16, pass_go_bonus: 1)
def rent(property, owns_full_colour_set:)
  owns_full_colour_set ? property.price * 2 : property.price
end
```
Every number from the brief lives here, with **default keyword values**. Tests use `Rules.new(player_names: %w[Ann Bob], starting_money: 2)` to set up small scenarios. Changing a rule (rent = 2× price, a $2 GO bonus, five players) is done here.

### `game.rb` (the engine)

```ruby
def initialize(board:, rolls:, rules: Rules.new)
  @players = rules.player_names.map { |name| Player.new(name: name, money: rules.starting_money, position: start) }
  @owners = {}                      # { PropertySpace => Player }
```
`rules: Rules.new` is a default argument, a simple form of **dependency injection**: tests can pass in different rules.

`@owners` is the only ownership state. It's keyed by the space **object**, and Ruby hashes compare plain objects by identity by default, so two squares with the same name can't be mixed up.

```ruby
def play
  @rolls.each_with_index do |roll, turn|
    play_turn(@players[turn % @players.size], roll)   # 0,1,2,3,0,1... turn order
    @rolls_played += 1
    break if @players.any?(&:bankrupt?)               # stop at first bankruptcy
  end
  build_result
end
```

```ruby
def play_turn(player, roll)
  player.position, go_passes = board.advance(player.position, roll)  # multiple assignment
  player.receive(go_passes * @rules.pass_go_bonus)                   # GO bonus BEFORE landing (assumption 5)
  board[player.position].land(self, player)                           # space decides what happens
end
```
That first line uses **multiple assignment**: `advance` returns `[to, passes]`, Ruby unpacks the array, and `player.position = to` calls the `attr_accessor` setter.

**Public "services" the spaces call** (they sit above `private`, so spaces can call them):
- `buy`: `paid = player.pay(price)`. Ownership is only recorded if the full price was paid. If the player is short, they lose their money and the property stays unowned.
- `charge_rent`: `owner.receive(payer.pay(rent))`. The owner receives only what was actually paid.
- `owns_full_colour_set?`: `board.colour_group(colour).all? { |p| owner_of(p) == owner }`

`winners`: remove bankrupt players, find the highest `money`, and return everyone who has it. That gives a list, which handles ties.

### `result.rb`

```ruby
PlayerResult = Struct.new(:name, :money, :space, :bankrupt, keyword_init: true)
```
A `Struct` is a quick data class with readers built in. `keyword_init: true` lets you call `PlayerResult.new(name: ..., money: ...)`.

- `to_h` builds the hash for `--json`. `JSON.pretty_generate` in the CLI turns it into text.
- `summary` builds the plain-text output. `format('  %-10s $%-4d', ...)` works like C's printf: `%-10s` left-aligns a string in 10 characters.
- Keeping presentation here means `Game` never deals with printing.

### `cli.rb`

```ruby
json = !@argv.delete('--json').nil?
```
`Array#delete` removes the item and returns it, or nil if it wasn't there. So this line both detects the flag and strips it out, which lets `--json` appear anywhere in the arguments. Then `board_path, rolls_path = @argv` unpacks the two remaining arguments.

- `rescue Error => e` catches any of your custom errors and prints one clean line instead of a stack trace. That gives exit code 1; wrong arguments give 2.
- `out: $stdout, err: $stderr`: tests pass a `StringIO` (an in-memory "file") to capture the output.

---

## 4. The tests (minitest)

| File | What it covers |
|---|---|
| [test_helper.rb](test/test_helper.rb) | Puts `lib` on the load path, loads minitest and the app. `small_board` is a 5-square board that makes the arithmetic easy. |
| [board_test.rb](test/board_test.rb) | Loading and validating boards, every `advance` edge case (exact GO, leaving GO, multiple laps) |
| [game_test.rb](test/game_test.rb) | Each business rule in isolation, using 2 players and small amounts of money |
| [cli_test.rb](test/cli_test.rb) | JSON shape, argument order, error messages and exit codes, running the real executable |
| [scenario_test.rb](test/scenario_test.rb) | Whole games: rolls_1 and rolls_2 (guarding against regressions) and rolls_3 (worked out by hand) |

Minitest basics: a test class inherits `Minitest::Test`, every method whose name starts with `test_` runs, and you check results with `assert_equal expected, actual`, `assert_raises(SomeError) { ... }` and `assert_match(/regex/, str)`. `include TestHelpers` mixes the helper methods into the class (a **mixin**).

**Your machine:** 44 of the 45 tests pass on Ruby 3.4. The one error is `test_the_executable_runs_end_to_end` ([cli_test.rb:68](test/cli_test.rb:68)). Windows can't run a file directly from its `#!` line, so it raises `Errno::ENOEXEC`. The usual fix is to launch the script through Ruby itself: `Open3.capture2(RbConfig.ruby, BIN, ...)`. Run the tests and the program like this:

```bash
ruby -Ilib -Itest -e 'Dir["test/*_test.rb"].each { |f| require "./#{f}" }'
```
```bash
ruby bin/woven_monopoly data/board.json data/rolls_1.json --json
```

**Config files:**
- `Gemfile`: development-only gems (minitest, rake, rubocop). The program itself uses only Ruby's standard library, as the brief asks.
- `Rakefile`: defines `rake test`.
- `.rubocop.yml`: linter settings, targeting Ruby 3.1 because they run JRuby. It has **never been run**, so run `bundle exec rubocop` before you submit.

---

## 5. One turn, traced (rolls_3, roll 6: Billy rolls 6)

1. `play`: turn index 5, and `5 % 4 = 1`, so it's Billy's turn.
2. `advance(1, 6)`: `to = 7` (Gami Chicken), `distance_to_go = (0-1) % 9 = 8`, `6 < 8`, so 0 passes.
3. `receive(0 * 1)`: no bonus.
4. `board[7].land(game, billy)`: the owner is Peter, not Billy, so `charge_rent`.
5. `owns_full_colour_set?(peter, Gami)`: Peter owns both Blue properties, so true, and `rent` = 4 × 2 = **$8**.
6. `billy.pay(8)` returns 8 and Billy is not bankrupt. `peter.receive(8)`.

Try the whole rolls_3 table in the README by hand. AI_USAGE.md asks you to do exactly this.

---

## 6. Interview prep: where likely new rules would go

| Likely request | Where to change it |
|---|---|
| Add a Tax / Jail / Free Parking square | New `Space` subclass with its own `land`, plus one entry in `SPACE_TYPES` |
| Rent = 2× price, or rent from a JSON field | `Rules#rent` (or `PropertySpace.build` for a new field) |
| $2 for passing GO, or no bonus for landing exactly on GO | `Rules`, or the `distance_to_go` logic in `Board#advance` |
| Keep playing after a bankruptcy | `Game#play` (the `break`) and `winners` |
| A bankrupt player's properties go to the creditor | `Game#charge_rent` |
| Print a log of each turn | Record events in `Game#play_turn`, display them in `Result`/`CLI` |

One last thing: [AI_USAGE.md](AI_USAGE.md) still has **TODO (Nivethaa)** sections. They need to be written in your own words, and one asks you to rewrite part of the code yourself. Fixing that Windows test yourself would be a real, small example for it.

I can also turn this guide into a page you can keep open while you study.

using System.Text.Json;

namespace WovenMonopoly;

public sealed class Board
{
    private readonly List<Space> _spaces;
    public int GoIndex { get; }
    public int Size => _spaces.Count;
    public Space this[int index] => _spaces[index];

    private Board(List<Space> spaces, int goIndex)
    {
        _spaces = spaces;
        GoIndex = goIndex;
    }

    public static Board Load(string path)
    {
        string text;
        try { text = File.ReadAllText(path); }
        catch (IOException exception) { throw new GameInputException($"could not read board file '{path}': {exception.Message}"); }
        catch (UnauthorizedAccessException exception) { throw new GameInputException($"could not read board file '{path}': {exception.Message}"); }

        try
        {
            using var document = JsonDocument.Parse(text);
            if (document.RootElement.ValueKind != JsonValueKind.Array)
                throw new GameInputException("board must be a JSON array of spaces");

            var spaces = new List<Space>();
            foreach (var item in document.RootElement.EnumerateArray())
            {
                if (item.ValueKind != JsonValueKind.Object)
                    throw new GameInputException($"each space must be an object, got {item}");
                var type = RequiredString(item, "type");
                var name = RequiredString(item, "name");
                switch (type)
                {
                    case "go":
                        spaces.Add(new GoSpace(name));
                        break;
                    case "property":
                        if (!item.TryGetProperty("price", out var priceElement) ||
                            !priceElement.TryGetInt32(out var price) || price <= 0)
                            throw new GameInputException($"space '{name}': price must be a positive integer");
                        spaces.Add(new PropertySpace(name, price, RequiredString(item, "colour")));
                        break;
                    default:
                        throw new GameInputException($"unknown space type '{type}'");
                }
            }

            var goIndexes = spaces.Select((space, index) => (space, index))
                .Where(pair => pair.space is GoSpace).Select(pair => pair.index).ToList();
            if (goIndexes.Count != 1)
                throw new GameInputException($"board must have exactly one GO space, found {goIndexes.Count}");
            return new Board(spaces, goIndexes[0]);
        }
        catch (JsonException exception)
        {
            throw new GameInputException($"board is not valid JSON: {exception.Message}");
        }
    }

    public (int Position, int GoPasses) Advance(int from, int steps)
    {
        if (from < 0 || from >= Size) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(from));
        if (steps < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(steps));
        var distanceToGo = (GoIndex - from + Size) % Size;
        if (distanceToGo == 0) distanceToGo = Size; // Starting on GO is not passing it.
        var passes = steps < distanceToGo ? 0 : 1 + (steps - distanceToGo) / Size;
        return ((from + steps) % Size, passes);
    }

    public List<PropertySpace> ColourGroup(string colour) => _spaces
        .OfType<PropertySpace>().Where(space => space.Colour == colour).ToList();

    private static string RequiredString(JsonElement item, string key)
    {
        if (!item.TryGetProperty(key, out var value) || value.ValueKind != JsonValueKind.String ||
            string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(value.GetString()))
            throw new GameInputException($"space is missing a valid '{key}' string");
        return value.GetString()!;
    }
}


public abstract class Space
{
    public string Name { get; }

    public Space(string name)
    {
        Name = name;
    }
}
public sealed class GoSpace : Space
{
    public GoSpace(string name) : base(name)
    {
    }
}
public sealed class PropertySpace : Space
{
    public int Price { get; }
    public string Colour { get; }

    public PropertySpace(string name, int price, string colour)
        : base(name)
    {
        Price = price;
        Colour = colour;
    }
}
public sealed class GameInputException : Exception
{
    public GameInputException(string message) : base(message)
    {
    }
}

This C# is a port of two Ruby files: [board.rb](woven_monopoly/lib/woven_monopoly/board.rb) and [space.rb](woven_monopoly/lib/woven_monopoly/space.rb). Comparing them is a quick way to learn the Ruby, so here is how they line up and where they behave differently.

## How the C# maps to the Ruby

| C# | Ruby | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `namespace WovenMonopoly;` | `module WovenMonopoly ... end` | Same idea. Ruby uses a block instead of a file-wide statement. |
| `public int GoIndex { get; }` | `attr_reader :go_index` | A read-only property is a getter generated by `attr_reader`. |
| `public int Size => _spaces.Count;` | `def size; @spaces.size; end` | Ruby has no separate property syntax. A method with no arguments called without `()` does the same job. |
| `public Space this[int index]` | `def [](index) @spaces.fetch(index) end` | Both define `board[3]`. Both throw on a bad index. Ruby's plain `[]` would return `nil`, which is why it uses `fetch`. |
| `private Board(...)` + `static Load` | `def self.from_file` / `from_json` / `from_array` | C# has one big factory. Ruby splits it into three steps (file → text → array), so tests can skip the file and call `from_array` directly. |
| The `try`/`catch` blocks | Method-level `rescue Errno::ENOENT` | In Ruby, a `def` can end with `rescue` without a `begin`. |
| `(int Position, int GoPasses)` tuple | `[to, passes]` array | Ruby returns an array, and the caller unpacks it: `player.position, go_passes = board.advance(...)`. |
| `OfType<PropertySpace>().Where(...)` | `select { \|s\| s.is_a?(PropertySpace) && s.colour == colour }` | `is_a?` is Ruby's `is`. `select` is `Where`. |
| `Select((space, index) => ...)` | `each_index.select { \|i\| ... }` | Same "find the positions of GO" logic. |
| `GameInputException` | `InvalidBoardError < Error < StandardError` | Ruby has a small hierarchy, so the CLI's single `rescue Error` catches both board and rolls errors. |
| `abstract` / `sealed` | (nothing) | Ruby has neither. Anyone can create a plain `Space` or subclass `PropertySpace`. |

## The modulo detail in `Advance`

```csharp
var distanceToGo = (GoIndex - from + Size) % Size;   // C#
```
```ruby
distance_to_go = (@go_index - from) % size            # Ruby
```
The C# needs `+ Size` because C#'s `%` keeps the sign: `(0 - 8) % 9` is `-8`. Ruby's `%` always returns a non-negative result when the divisor is positive, so `(0 - 8) % 9` is `1`. If anyone asks why there's no `+ size` in the Ruby version, this is the answer.

## Where the two versions behave differently

1. **Adding a new kind of square.** The C# uses a `switch (type)` inside `Board.Load`, so a new square type means editing `Board`. The Ruby keeps a registry instead, `SPACE_TYPES = { 'go' => GoSpace, 'property' => PropertySpace }`, and each class has its own `self.build(attrs)`. A new square is a new class plus one hash entry, and `Board` barely changes. This is the extensibility the brief asks for.

2. **The C# `Space` has no behaviour.** The Ruby `Space` has `land(game, player)`, and `PropertySpace` overrides it to buy or charge rent. With the C# classes, the game loop would need `if (space is PropertySpace p) ...`, and that check would grow with every new square type. If you're porting the whole game, the C# equivalent is `public virtual void Land(Game game, Player player) {}` on `Space`, with an `override` in `PropertySpace`.

3. **The C# file handling is more thorough.** It catches `IOException` (which includes file not found) and `UnauthorizedAccessException`. The Ruby only rescues `Errno::ENOENT` (not found) and `Errno::EISDIR` (a folder instead of a file). So in Ruby, a board file you don't have permission to read crashes with a stack trace instead of the clean one-line error. Adding `Errno::EACCES` to that `rescue` line would fix it.

4. **Guards in `Advance`.** The C# rejects an out-of-range `from` and a negative `steps`, and allows `steps == 0`. The Ruby `advance` checks nothing itself. `Game#validate_rolls` rejects any roll that isn't a positive whole number before play starts. The safety is the same, but it lives in a different place.

5. **Small validation differences.**
   - C# rejects blank names (`IsNullOrWhiteSpace`). Ruby only checks that `name` is a String, so `""` is accepted.
   - C# checks `type` and `name` before the switch, so `{"type":"jail"}` with no name reports a missing name. Ruby reports "unknown space type".
   - Ruby's error messages include the space name (`space "Massizim": 'price' must be...`). The C# `RequiredString` messages don't.

6. **Style nit in the C#.** The constructor of an `abstract` class is usually `protected`, not `public`, since nothing outside can call it anyway.

Was this C# meant as a reference for reading the Ruby, or are you porting the whole game to C#? If you're porting, I can sketch the `Land` method, `Player`, `Rules` and the game loop next.

content.text:
This file sets up the **game board** and the **squares** on it. It doesn't play the game. It reads the board and answers questions about it.

## What the file contains

**1. Square types (`Space`, `GoSpace`, `PropertySpace`)**
- **Space** is any square on the board. Every square has a name.
- **GoSpace** is the starting square (GO).
- **PropertySpace** is a square that can be bought. It has a name, a **price** and a **colour**, for example "Massizim, $4, Blue".

These classes only hold information. They don't do anything when a player lands on them.

**2. The board (`Board`)**

The board is the list of squares in order. It can do four things:

- **Load the board from a file (`Load`).** It opens `board.json`, reads each square and creates the right kind of square object. It also checks the file is correct:
  - the file exists and can be opened
  - it's valid JSON and is a list
  - every square has a type and a name
  - every property has a price above 0 and a colour
  - there are no unknown square types
  - there is exactly one GO square

  If anything is wrong, it stops with a clear error message.

- **Move a player (`Advance`).** Given a starting square and a dice roll, it works out:
  - which square the player ends up on, going back to the start after the last square
  - how many times the player passed GO, so they can get $1 each time

  Landing exactly on GO counts as passing it. Starting on GO doesn't.

- **Find all properties of one colour (`ColourGroup`).** For example, "give me all the Blue properties". The game uses this to check whether one owner has the full colour set, which doubles the rent.

- **Basic lookups.** `Size` gives the number of squares, `GoIndex` gives where GO is, and `board[3]` gives the square at position 3.

**3. The error type (`GameInputException`)**

This is the special error raised when the board file is bad, so the program can show a simple message instead of crashing.

## In one sentence

The file **reads the board, checks it's valid, and works out where a player lands and whether they passed GO**. Buying, paying rent and taking turns happen in other files.

content.text:
I'll start from zero and use the real sample board as the example throughout.

## First, the board itself

`board.json` describes 9 squares in a loop. Each square has a **position number**, starting from 0:

```
 0: GO
 1: The Burvale        ($1, Brown)
 2: Fast Kebabs        ($1, Brown)
 3: The Grand Tofu     ($2, Red)
 4: Lanzhou Beef Noodle($2, Red)
 5: Betty's Burgers    ($3, Green)
 6: YOMG               ($3, Green)
 7: Gami Chicken       ($4, Blue)
 8: Massizim           ($4, Blue)
 → after 8, you go back to 0
```

Players never hold the square itself. They hold a **number**, their position. "Peter is at 7" means Peter is on Gami Chicken.

---

## Why `Load` builds a `Board` object

**The problem:** `board.json` is just text in a file. The program can't ask text questions like "what's the price of square 3?"

**What `Load` does:** it turns that text into objects the program can use:

1. **Read the file** into a string (`File.ReadAllText`). If the file is missing, report an error.
2. **Parse the JSON** so the text becomes a list of entries.
3. **Go through each entry** and create the right kind of object:
   - `"type": "go"` creates `new GoSpace("GO")`
   - `"type": "property"` creates `new PropertySpace("Massizim", 4, "Blue")`
   - anything else is an error: "unknown space type"
4. **Find where GO is** in the list. This becomes `GoIndex`.
5. **Package the list and GoIndex together** into one `Board` object and return it.

**Why bother with a `Board` object instead of passing a plain list around?** Two reasons:

- **Everything about the board is in one place.** The rest of the program just says `board[3]`, `board.Size` or `board.Advance(...)` and doesn't need to know how the board is stored.
- **A broken board can never exist.** The constructor is `private Board(...)`, so no other code can write `new Board(...)`. The only way to get a board is through `Load`, which checks everything first (exactly one GO, prices above 0, and so on). If you're holding a `Board`, you know it's valid.

In [Program.cs:20](Program.cs:20) it's used like this:
```csharp
var board = Board.Load(paths[0]);   // "board.json" → Board object
```

---

## What `GoIndex` is

**`GoIndex` is the position number of the GO square.** On the sample board GO is first, so `GoIndex = 0`.

**Why not just assume GO is at 0?** The brief says they'll test with boards you haven't seen. Someone could put GO in the middle:

```
0: Tofu   1: Kebabs   2: GO   3: Massizim
```
Here `GoIndex = 2`. The code *searches* for GO instead of guessing.

**What it's used for:**
1. **Starting position.** Every player starts on GO ([Game.cs:23](Game.cs:23) passes `board.GoIndex` as each player's position).
2. **Counting GO passes** inside `Advance`, to decide when to pay the $1 bonus.

---

## What `Advance` does

**Question it answers:** "A player is on square X and rolls Y. Which square do they end on, and how many times did they pass GO?"

It returns **two answers**: `(Position, GoPasses)`.

```csharp
public (int Position, int GoPasses) Advance(int from, int steps)
{
    // safety checks: from must be on the board, steps can't be negative
    var distanceToGo = (GoIndex - from + Size) % Size;   // ① how far away is GO?
    if (distanceToGo == 0) distanceToGo = Size;          // ② standing ON GO → next GO is a full lap away
    var passes = steps < distanceToGo ? 0                // ③ didn't reach GO → 0 passes
               : 1 + (steps - distanceToGo) / Size;      //    reached GO → 1, plus 1 per extra full lap
    return ((from + steps) % Size, passes);              // ④ where you land, wrapping around
}
```

**`%` (the remainder) is what makes the board wrap around.** With 9 squares, `11 % 9 = 2`, so moving to "square 11" really means square 2.

### Example 1: a normal move (no GO)
Peter is on **1** (Burvale) and rolls **3**.
- ① distance to GO = `(0 - 1 + 9) % 9 = 8`, so GO is 8 steps away
- ③ 3 is less than 8, so **0 passes**
- ④ land on `(1 + 3) % 9 = 4`, **Lanzhou Beef Noodle**
- Result: `(4, 0)`

### Example 2: going past the end
Billy is on **8** (Massizim) and rolls **3**.
- ① distance to GO = `(0 - 8 + 9) % 9 = 1`, so GO is the very next square
- ③ 3 is at least 1, so `1 + (3 - 1) / 9 = 1 + 0` = **1 pass**
- ④ land on `(8 + 3) % 9 = 2`, **Fast Kebabs**
- Result: `(2, 1)`, so Billy gets $1

### Example 3: landing exactly on GO
Charlotte is on **7** and rolls **2**.
- ① distance to GO = `(0 - 7 + 9) % 9 = 2`
- ③ 2 is at least 2, so **1 pass** (landing on GO counts)
- ④ land on `(7 + 2) % 9 = 0`, **GO**
- Result: `(0, 1)`

### Example 4: starting on GO
Everyone starts on 0. Sweedal rolls **4**.
- ① distance to GO = `(0 - 0 + 9) % 9 = 0`
- ② 0 means "I'm standing on GO", so the next GO is a full lap away: distance becomes **9**
- ③ 4 is less than 9, so **0 passes**. Leaving GO doesn't earn the bonus, as the brief says.
- Result: `(4, 0)`

### Example 5: a huge roll
From **0**, roll **20**. Distance to GO is 9, so passes = `1 + (20 - 9) / 9 = 1 + 1 = 2`. The player went around twice and lands on `20 % 9 = 2`. Result: `(2, 2)`, which pays $2.

**Why `+ Size` in step ①?** In C#, `-8 % 9` gives `-8`, which isn't a valid square. Adding `Size` first gives `(-8 + 9) % 9 = 1`. (Ruby doesn't need this, because its `%` never returns a negative number here.)

### How the game uses it ([Game.cs:59-61](Game.cs:59))
```csharp
var (position, goPasses) = _board.Advance(player.Position, _rolls[turn]);  // ask the board
player.Position = position;                                              // move the player
player.Receive(goPasses * PassGoBonus);                                  // pay $1 per GO pass
ResolveLanding(player);                                                  // then buy or pay rent
```
The board only does the **counting**. It never touches money. The game takes the answer and pays the bonus.

---

## Summary

| Thing | Simple meaning |
|---|---|
| `Board` | The board: an ordered list of squares that loops around |
| `Load` | Reads `board.json`, checks it, and creates the `Board` |
| `GoIndex` | The square number where GO is. Players start there, and it's used to count GO passes. |
| `Size` | How many squares there are (9) |
| `board[3]` | "Give me square number 3" |
| `Advance` | "From square X, roll Y: where do I land, and how many times did I pass GO?" |
| `ColourGroup` | "Give me all the Blue properties", used to check for double rent |

A good way to make it stick: pick a few rolls from `rolls_1.json` and work out `Advance` by hand on paper, the way the examples above do.

# Woven Monopoly (C# study copy)

A C# translation of the Ruby project in `../woven_monopoly`, written to help read the Ruby code.
It behaves identically: same rules, same assumptions, same output for all three roll files.
The Ruby version is the one to submit; the brief prefers Ruby.

```
dotnet run --project src/WovenMonopoly -- data/board.json data/rolls_1.json --json
```

```
dotnet test
```

## Layout (Models / Views / Controllers)

| C# file | Ruby file | Job |
|---|---|---|
| `src/WovenMonopoly/Program.cs` | `bin/woven_monopoly` | Entry point: hands the arguments to the controller, returns its exit code |
| `Controllers/GameController.cs` | `lib/woven_monopoly/cli.rb` | Reads arguments, loads the two files, runs the game, picks a view |
| `Models/Errors.cs` | `errors.rb` | Error types for bad input |
| `Models/Space.cs` | `space.rb` | `Space`, `GoSpace`, `PropertySpace`: what happens when you land on a square |
| `Models/Board.cs` | `board.rb` | Squares in order, loading `board.json`, `Advance`, colour groups |
| `Models/Player.cs` | `player.rb` | Name, money, position, bankrupt flag |
| `Models/Rules.cs` | `rules.rb` | Starting money, GO bonus, player names, rent formula |
| `Models/Game.cs` | `game.rb` | The turn loop and who owns what |
| `Models/GameResult.cs` | `result.rb` (data part) | The finished game as plain data |
| `Views/SummaryView.cs` | `Result#summary` | Plain-text output |
| `Views/JsonView.cs` | `Result#to_h` | `--json` output |
| `tests/WovenMonopoly.Tests/*` | `test/*` | The same 45 tests, in xUnit |

The one structural difference: in Ruby, `Result` both holds the data and prints itself. In MVC the
data is a Model (`GameResult`) and each output format is a View.

## Ruby to C# cheat sheet

| Ruby | C# |
|---|---|
| `module WovenMonopoly` | `namespace WovenMonopoly.Models;` |
| `attr_reader :name` | `public string Name { get; }` |
| `attr_accessor :position` | `public int Position { get; set; }` |
| `def self.build(attrs)` | `public static Space Build(JsonElement attrs)` |
| `def initialize(name:, money:)` | constructor `Player(string name, int money)` |
| `def bankrupt?` | `bool IsBankrupt` |
| `raise InvalidBoardError, "..."` / `rescue` | `throw new InvalidBoardException("...")` / `catch` |
| `@owners = {}` | `Dictionary<PropertySpace, Player> _owners` |
| `players.map(&:name)` | `players.Select(p => p.Name)` |
| `players.select { ... }` / `.all?` / `.any?` | `.Where(...)` / `.All(...)` / `.Any(...)` |
| `return [to, passes]` and `a, b = advance(...)` | return a tuple `(to, passes)` and `var (a, b) = Advance(...)` |
| `Rules.new(starting_money: 2)` | `new Rules { StartingMoney = 2 }` |
| `x % n` (never negative) | `(x + n) % n` (C#'s `%` can be negative) |
| `owner&.name` | `owner?.Name` |

content.text:
You've got the main idea right. It reads `rolls.json`, takes each value, puts it into `roll`, and builds an array. The checks are there because **the file might contain something that isn't a list of dice rolls**, and the method has to catch that before the game starts.

It works in three stages. Each stage has its own check.

## Stage 1: read the file

```csharp
try { text = File.ReadAllText(path); }
catch (IOException exception) { throw new GameInputException(...); }
catch (UnauthorizedAccessException exception) { throw new GameInputException(...); }
```
**Question:** can we open the file at all?
- `IOException`: the file doesn't exist, or the folder is wrong.
- `UnauthorizedAccessException`: you don't have permission to read it, or the path is a folder.

If either happens, it throws a `GameInputException` with a friendly message. `Program.cs` catches that and prints `Error: could not read rolls file ...` instead of crashing.

## Stage 2: is it valid JSON, and is it a list?

```csharp
using var document = JsonDocument.Parse(text);          // check 2a
if (document.RootElement.ValueKind != JsonValueKind.Array)   // check 2b
    throw new GameInputException("rolls must be a JSON array ...");
```
- **2a, `JsonDocument.Parse`:** turns the text into JSON. If the text is broken, like `[1, 2,` with no closing bracket, it throws `JsonException`, and the `catch (JsonException ...)` at the bottom turns that into "rolls file is not valid JSON".
- **2b, `ValueKind != Array`:** the JSON is valid but isn't a list. For example `{"rolls": 5}` is a JSON object, not an array.

`RootElement` means the top-level thing in the file. For `[1, 3, 1]`, the root element is the whole list.

## Stage 3: check each value and collect them

```csharp
return document.RootElement.EnumerateArray().Select(element =>
{
    if (!element.TryGetInt32(out var roll) || roll <= 0)
        throw new GameInputException("rolls must be ... positive whole numbers");
    return roll;
}).ToArray();
```
- `EnumerateArray()` goes through each item in the list, one at a time.
- `.Select(element => { ... })` runs the code inside the braces for every item and keeps whatever it `return`s.
- `.ToArray()` collects all the returned values into an `int[]`.

**The check, piece by piece:**

```csharp
element.TryGetInt32(out var roll)
```
"Try" methods in C# do two things at once:
- they **return** `true` or `false`, meaning "did it work?"
- if it worked, they **put the number into `roll`**. That's what `out` means: the method fills the variable for you.

So for the item `4`, it returns `true` and `roll` becomes `4`. For `1.5`, it returns `false`, because 1.5 isn't a whole number.

```csharp
if (!worked || roll <= 0)  throw ...
```
- `!` means "not", so `!worked` means "it did NOT turn into a whole number".
- `||` means "or".
- `roll <= 0` rejects 0 and negative numbers, because you can't move 0 or −3 squares.

In plain English: **"if this item isn't a whole number, or it's zero or less, stop with an error. Otherwise keep it."**

## Examples

| `rolls.json` contains | What happens |
|---|---|
| `[1, 3, 1]` | All good, returns `int[] { 1, 3, 1 }` |
| file missing | Stage 1: "could not read rolls file" |
| `[1, 2,` | Stage 2a: "not valid JSON" |
| `{"a": 1}` | Stage 2b: "must be a JSON array" |
| `[1, 1.5]` | Stage 3: `TryGetInt32` is false, error |
| `[1, 0]` or `[1, -2]` | Stage 3: `roll <= 0`, error |
| `[1, "2"]` or `[1, null]` | **Crash.** See the bug below. |

## A bug in this code

`TryGetInt32` only works on items that are **numbers**. If an item is text (`"2"`) or `null`, it doesn't return `false`. It throws `InvalidOperationException` instead. Nothing catches that, so the program crashes with a stack trace instead of printing the clean error.

The fix is to check that the item is a number first:
```csharp
if (element.ValueKind != JsonValueKind.Number || !element.TryGetInt32(out var roll) || roll <= 0)
    throw new GameInputException("rolls must be a JSON array of positive whole numbers");
```
`||` stops at the first `true`. So for `"2"`, the first part, "not a number", is already true, and C# never calls `TryGetInt32`. The C# copy I built does this check in `IsWholeNumber` in [GameController.cs](WovenMonopolyMvc/src/WovenMonopoly/Controllers/GameController.cs), and the test `ABadRollsFileIsACleanError` covers `"2"` and `null`.

## The same method in Ruby

```ruby
def load_rolls(path)
  JSON.parse(File.read(path))                       # stage 1 + 2a
rescue Errno::ENOENT, Errno::EISDIR
  raise InvalidRollsError, "rolls file not found: #{path}"
rescue JSON::ParserError => e
  raise InvalidRollsError, "rolls file is not valid JSON: #{e.message}"
end
```
In Ruby, the stage 2b and stage 3 checks are done separately, in `Game#validate_rolls`:
```ruby
rolls.is_a?(Array) && rolls.all? { |r| r.is_a?(Integer) && r.positive? }
```
That one line means: "it's a list, **and** every item is a whole number **and** greater than 0." It's the same check as the C#, written much shorter.

You've understood it correctly. `ResolveLanding` runs right after a player moves, and it decides what happens on the square they landed on. The confusing part is `!_owners.TryGetValue(...)`, so let's break it into pieces.

## 1. What `_owners` is

```csharp
private readonly Dictionary<PropertySpace, Player> _owners = [];
```
A **Dictionary** is a lookup table: you give it a **key** and get back a **value**. Here:
- **key** = a property (a square)
- **value** = the player who owns it

Partway through a game it might look like this:

| Key (property) | Value (owner) |
|---|---|
| Gami Chicken | Peter |
| The Burvale | Billy |

A property that **nobody owns is simply not in the table**. At the start of the game the table is empty.

## 2. What `TryGetValue` does

```csharp
_owners.TryGetValue(property, out var owner)
```
In plain English: **"Look up this property in the table. Is it there?"**

Like `TryGetInt32` from before, it gives two answers:
- it **returns** `true` (found it) or `false` (not in the table)
- if found, it **puts the owner into the variable `owner`**. That's what `out var owner` does.

| Player lands on | TryGetValue returns | `owner` becomes |
|---|---|---|
| Gami Chicken | `true` | Peter |
| Massizim (not in table) | `false` | `null` (nobody) |

## 3. What the `!` means

`!` means **NOT**. It flips true and false.

```csharp
if (!_owners.TryGetValue(property, out var owner))
```
reads as: **"if this property is NOT found in the owners table"**, which means **"if nobody owns it yet"**.

It's not saying anything about the owner. The `!` applies to the whole `TryGetValue(...)` result, the true/false answer.

## The whole method in plain English

```csharp
if (_board[player.Position] is not PropertySpace property) return;
```
**"If this square is not a property (for example GO), there's nothing to do. Stop."**
If it *is* a property, the `property` variable now holds it, ready to use.

```csharp
if (!_owners.TryGetValue(property, out var owner))
{
    var paid = player.Pay(property.Price);
    if (paid == property.Price) _owners[property] = player;
    return;
}
```
**"If nobody owns it, the player must buy it."**
- `player.Pay(price)` takes the money and returns how much was actually paid.
- `if (paid == property.Price)`: only if they paid the full price...
- `_owners[property] = player` ...is a new row added to the table: "this property now belongs to this player".
- If they couldn't afford it, they're now bankrupt and nobody gets the property.
- `return` means stop here.

```csharp
if (owner == player) return;
```
**"If the player owns it themselves, nothing happens. Stop."**
At this point we know the property *was* found, so `owner` holds the real owner.

```csharp
var ownsGroup = _board.ColourGroup(property.Colour).All(space =>
    _owners.TryGetValue(space, out var groupOwner) && groupOwner == owner);
```
**"Does the owner own every property of this colour?"**
- `ColourGroup("Blue")` gives `[Gami Chicken, Massizim]`.
- `.All(...)` is true only if the check passes for **every** one of them.
- The check, for each square: "is it in the table **and** is its owner the same person?"

```csharp
var rent = property.Price * (ownsGroup ? 2 : 1);
owner.Receive(player.Pay(rent));
```
**"Rent is the price, doubled if they own the whole colour. The player pays and the owner receives."**
`player.Pay(rent)` runs first and returns what was paid, then `owner.Receive(...)` gets exactly that amount.

## As a flowchart

```
Player lands on a square
   │
   ├─ Not a property? ───────────────► do nothing
   │
   ├─ Nobody owns it? (!TryGetValue) ─► BUY it
   │
   ├─ I own it? (owner == player) ───► do nothing
   │
   └─ Someone else owns it ──────────► PAY RENT (×2 if they own the whole colour)
```

In my C# copy, the same steps are split up: `PropertySpace.Land` in [Space.cs](WovenMonopolyMvc/src/WovenMonopoly/Models/Space.cs) does the flowchart, and `Game.Buy` and `Game.ChargeRent` do the buying and paying. There, `game.OwnerOf(this)` returns the owner or `null`, so the check reads `if (owner is null)`. That's the same question as `!TryGetValue`, just easier to read.

Here is the whole program from start to finish, in the order it runs.

## 1. Where the program starts: `Program.cs`

You start it with:
```bash
dotnet run -- board.json rolls_1.json --json
```
[Program.cs](Program.cs) has no class and no `Main` method. That's a C# feature called **top-level statements**: the code at the top of this file *is* the starting point, and C# runs it from line 1 downwards.

`args` is the list of words after `--`, here `["board.json", "rolls_1.json", "--json"]`.

```
Program.cs line 4    --help?  → print usage, stop (return 0)
Program.cs line 10   remember if "--json" was given
Program.cs line 11   remove "--json" → paths = ["board.json", "rolls_1.json"]
Program.cs line 12   not exactly 2 paths? → print usage, stop (return 2)
```

Then the real work happens in **4 lines** ([Program.cs:20-26](Program.cs:20)):
```csharp
var board  = Board.Load(paths[0]);          // ① build the board
var rolls  = Game.LoadRolls(paths[1]);      // ② read the dice rolls
var result = new Game(board, rolls).Play(); // ③ create the game  ④ play it
Console.WriteLine(jsonOutput ? ... : result.Summary());  // ⑤ print the result
```
Everything else in the program is called from these lines.

---

## 2. Step ①: `Board.Load` creates the Board and the Space objects

[Board.cs:25](Board.cs:25). It reads `board.json`, and for each entry it creates a square object:
- `"go"` → `new GoSpace(name)` ([Board.cs:70](Board.cs:70))
- `"property"` → `new PropertySpace(name, price, colour)` ([Board.cs:82](Board.cs:82))

That gives **9 Space objects** in a list. It finds where GO is, then creates the board itself:
```csharp
return new Board(spaces, goIndexes[0]);   // Board.cs:114
```
Back in `Program.cs`, `board` now holds **1 Board object, which holds 9 Space objects**.

## 3. Step ②: `Game.LoadRolls` creates the rolls array

[Game.cs:26](Game.cs:26). It reads `rolls_1.json` and returns `int[] { 1, 3, 1, 1, 1, 2, ... }`. This is just numbers, not objects.

## 4. Step ③: `new Game(board, rolls)` creates the Game and the 4 Players

This is the part you asked about. The **Game constructor** ([Game.cs:17-24](Game.cs:17)) runs:
```csharp
public Game(Board board, int[] rolls)
{
    if (rolls.Any(roll => roll <= 0)) throw ...;   // check rolls
    _board = board;                                  // keep the board
    _rolls = rolls;                                  // keep the rolls
    _players = PlayerNames.Select(name => new Player(name, StartingMoney, board.GoIndex)).ToList();
}
```
The last line is **where the Player objects are born**. Read it like this:
- `PlayerNames` is `["Peter", "Billy", "Charlotte", "Sweedal"]` (line 7)
- `.Select(name => new Player(...))` means "for each name, create a Player"
- `.ToList()` collects them into a list

So it's the same as writing:
```csharp
_players = new List<Player>
{
    new Player("Peter",     16, 0),
    new Player("Billy",     16, 0),
    new Player("Charlotte", 16, 0),
    new Player("Sweedal",   16, 0),
};
```
(16 = `StartingMoney`, 0 = `board.GoIndex`, so everyone starts on GO.)

**What `new Player(...)` does** ([Game.cs:95](Game.cs:95)):
```csharp
public sealed class Player(string name, int money, int position)
{
    public string Name { get; } = name;              // "Peter"
    public int Money { get; private set; } = money;  // 16
    public int Position { get; set; } = position;    // 0
    public bool IsBankrupt { get; private set; }     // false (default)
```
The brackets after `class Player(...)` are a **primary constructor**, a short way of writing a constructor. The values you pass in are copied into the properties.

`Money` has `private set`. That means **only Player's own methods can change money**: `Pay` and `Receive`. Code outside can read `player.Money` but can't write `player.Money = 100`.

The game also starts with an empty ownership table: `_owners = []` (line 14).

## 5. Step ④: `.Play()` runs the game loop

[Game.cs:51](Game.cs:51). This is where `Pay` and `Receive` are actually called.

```csharp
for (var turn = 0; turn < _rolls.Length; turn++)
{
    var player = _players[turn % _players.Count];                        // whose turn?
    var (position, goPasses) = _board.Advance(player.Position, _rolls[turn]); // where do they land?
    player.Position = position;                                          // move them
    player.Receive(goPasses * PassGoBonus);                              // ← RECEIVE: GO bonus
    ResolveLanding(player);                                              // buy or pay rent
    rollsPlayed++;
    if (player.IsBankrupt) break;                                        // stop if bankrupt
}
```

**Whose turn:** `turn % 4` gives 0, 1, 2, 3, 0, 1, 2, 3... which is Peter, Billy, Charlotte, Sweedal, Peter...

**`ResolveLanding(player)`** ([Game.cs:77](Game.cs:77)) is where money moves:
- **Buy:** `player.Pay(property.Price)`, and the property is added to `_owners`
- **Rent:** `owner.Receive(player.Pay(rent))`, so the player pays and the owner receives

### Every place Pay and Receive are called

| Call | Where | When |
|---|---|---|
| `player.Receive(goPasses * 1)` | `Play`, line 61 | every turn (adds $0 if GO wasn't passed) |
| `player.Pay(price)` | `ResolveLanding`, line 82 | buying an unowned property |
| `player.Pay(rent)` | `ResolveLanding`, line 91 | landing on someone else's property |
| `owner.Receive(...)` | `ResolveLanding`, line 91 | the owner collecting rent |

## 6. Step ④, continued: building the result

After the loop ([Game.cs:67-74](Game.cs:67)):
- it finds the winners: players who aren't bankrupt and have the most money
- it creates one `PlayerResult` per player (name, money, square name, bankrupt)
- it creates one `GameResult` and returns it to `Program.cs`

## 7. Step ⑤: print and exit

Back in `Program.cs`: if `--json` was given, `JsonSerializer.Serialize(result)` prints JSON. Otherwise `result.Summary()` prints the text version. Then `return 0` ends the program successfully.

If anything threw a `GameInputException` along the way (bad file, bad JSON, bad roll), the `catch` at line 29 prints `Error: ...` and returns 1.

---

## All the objects at once

```
Program.cs
 ├─ board  ──► Board
 │              └─ _spaces: [GoSpace, PropertySpace × 8]
 ├─ rolls  ──► int[] {1, 3, 1, 1, ...}
 └─ new Game(board, rolls)
               ├─ _board   ──► (the same Board as above)
               ├─ _rolls   ──► (the same array)
               ├─ _players ──► [Player Peter, Player Billy, Player Charlotte, Player Sweedal]
               └─ _owners  ──► { PropertySpace → Player }   (starts empty, filled as players buy)
                    │
                  .Play()  ──► returns GameResult ──► printed by Program.cs
```

**An important idea:** `_owners` doesn't hold copies of the players. It holds **references to the same 4 Player objects** that are in `_players`. So when the code runs `owner.Receive(2)` using the owner from `_owners`, it's Peter's one and only object whose money goes up. That's why the final result shows the right amounts.

This line answers one question: **"Does the owner own every property of this colour?"** Let's take it apart.

```csharp
var ownsGroup = _board.ColourGroup(property.Colour).All(space =>
    _owners.TryGetValue(space, out var groupOwner) && groupOwner == owner);
```

## Piece 1: `_board.ColourGroup(property.Colour)`

This gives back a **list of all properties with that colour**.

If the player landed on Gami Chicken (Blue):
```
ColourGroup("Blue")  →  [Gami Chicken, Massizim]
```

## Piece 2: `.All( ... )`

`.All` asks a **yes/no question about every item in the list**:
- if the answer is **yes for every item**, `.All` returns `true`
- if the answer is **no for even one item**, `.All` returns `false`

Think of a teacher checking: "Did **all** students hand in homework?" One missing student means the answer is no.

## Piece 3: `space => ...` is the question

```csharp
space => _owners.TryGetValue(space, out var groupOwner) && groupOwner == owner
```
This is a **lambda**, a tiny unnamed function. `.All` calls it once for each item in the list, and each time `space` is the current item.

- 1st call: `space` = Gami Chicken
- 2nd call: `space` = Massizim

The question it asks about each `space` has two parts joined by `&&` ("and"):

| Part | Plain English |
|---|---|
| `_owners.TryGetValue(space, out var groupOwner)` | "Does anyone own this square?" If yes, put that person into `groupOwner`. |
| `groupOwner == owner` | "Is that person the **same owner** we're charging rent for?" |

Both parts must be true. If nobody owns the square, the first part is false and the answer for that square is **no**.

## The same code written as a normal loop

Maybe this version is easier to read. It does exactly the same thing:

```csharp
bool ownsGroup = true;                                   // assume yes

List<PropertySpace> sameColour = _board.ColourGroup(property.Colour);

foreach (PropertySpace space in sameColour)
{
    bool someoneOwnsIt = _owners.TryGetValue(space, out Player? groupOwner);

    if (!someoneOwnsIt)            // nobody owns this one
    {
        ownsGroup = false;
        break;
    }

    if (groupOwner != owner)       // someone else owns this one
    {
        ownsGroup = false;
        break;
    }
}
// here, ownsGroup is true only if the owner has every square of the colour
```

`.All(...)` is just a short way of writing that loop.

## Examples

`owner` = Peter (he owns the square that was landed on, Gami Chicken).

**Case A: Peter owns both Blues**

| space | someone owns it? | who? | same as Peter? | answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gami Chicken | yes | Peter | yes | ✅ |
| Massizim | yes | Peter | yes | ✅ |

All ✅, so `ownsGroup = true` and the rent is **doubled**.

**Case B: nobody has bought Massizim yet**

| space | someone owns it? | who? | same as Peter? | answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gami Chicken | yes | Peter | yes | ✅ |
| Massizim | **no** | – | – | ❌ |

One ❌, so `ownsGroup = false` and the rent is **normal**.

**Case C: Billy owns Massizim**

| space | someone owns it? | who? | same as Peter? | answer |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gami Chicken | yes | Peter | yes | ✅ |
| Massizim | yes | Billy | **no** | ❌ |

One ❌, so `ownsGroup = false` and the rent is **normal**.

## How the result is used

```csharp
var rent = property.Price * (ownsGroup ? 2 : 1);
```
`? :` is a short if/else: **if `ownsGroup` is true use 2, otherwise use 1**. So Gami Chicken ($4) charges $8 in case A and $4 in cases B and C.

content.text:
These are the real values from running the game. Each block is one moment when a player lands on someone else's property. The indented lines show what `.All(...)` checks for each square of that colour.

## Case 1: nobody owns the other square yet → normal rent
From `rolls_1.json`:
```
Charlotte landed on The Burvale (Brown, $1)
   owner      = Peter
   sameColour = [The Burvale, Fast Kebabs]
      The Burvale    TryGetValue = True   groupOwner = Peter   same as owner? True
      Fast Kebabs    TryGetValue = False  groupOwner = null    same as owner? False
   ownsGroup  = False  ->  rent = 1 x 1 = $1
   after: Charlotte $15, Peter $16
```
- `owner` is **Peter**, because he owns The Burvale.
- `sameColour` is **both Brown squares**.
- Fast Kebabs isn't in `_owners`, so `TryGetValue = False` and `groupOwner = null`.
- One square fails, so `ownsGroup = False` and Charlotte pays normal rent: **$1**.

## Case 2: someone else owns the other square → normal rent
From `rolls_3.json`:
```
Billy landed on Lanzhou Beef Noodle (Red, $2)
   owner      = Charlotte
   sameColour = [The Grand Tofu, Lanzhou Beef Noodle]
      The Grand Tofu TryGetValue = True   groupOwner = Billy   same as owner? False
      Lanzhou Beef Noodle TryGetValue = True   groupOwner = Charlotte  same as owner? True
   ownsGroup  = False  ->  rent = 2 x 1 = $2
```
- Both squares are owned, so both `TryGetValue` calls are `True`, but **by different people**.
- The Grand Tofu's `groupOwner` is Billy, which isn't Charlotte, so `False`.
- `ownsGroup = False`, so the rent is normal: **$2**.

## Case 3: the owner has the whole colour → double rent
```
Charlotte landed on The Burvale (Brown, $1)
   owner      = Peter
   sameColour = [The Burvale, Fast Kebabs]
      The Burvale    TryGetValue = True   groupOwner = Peter   same as owner? True
      Fast Kebabs    TryGetValue = True   groupOwner = Peter   same as owner? True
   ownsGroup  = True  ->  rent = 1 x 2 = $2
   after: Charlotte $15, Peter $16
```
- Both checks are `True` and both owners are Peter.
- **Every** check passed, so `ownsGroup = True` and Charlotte pays **double** rent: $2.

Compare this with case 1: it's the same square and the same owner. The only difference is that Peter has since bought Fast Kebabs too.

## The pattern

```
.All( every square in sameColour → TryGetValue is True  AND  groupOwner == owner )
```
- **every** row says `same as owner? True` → `ownsGroup = True` → rent × 2
- **any** row says `False` → `ownsGroup = False` → rent × 1

## Doing this yourself

I made these changes in a scratch copy, so your project is untouched. You can find it at:
`C:\Users\NIVI\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\E--Pronto-woven-monopoly\310b4e49-85e9-4ca8-b7bc-36235f3d8ebc\scratchpad\codex_debug\Game.cs`

To try it in your own project, put these lines just before `var ownsGroup = ...` in `ResolveLanding`:
```csharp
Console.WriteLine($"{player.Name} landed on {property.Name}, owner = {owner.Name}");
foreach (var space in _board.ColourGroup(property.Colour))
{
    var found = _owners.TryGetValue(space, out var groupOwner);
    Console.WriteLine($"   {space.Name}: found = {found}, groupOwner = {groupOwner?.Name ?? "null"}");
}
```
Remove them again before you submit.

An even better tool for this is the **VS Code debugger**. Click left of the line number on `var ownsGroup = ...` to set a red-dot breakpoint, then press **F5**. The program pauses on that line, and you can hover over `owner`, `property` or `_owners` to see their values without adding any code.

Two other things I noticed while running it:
- The `rolls_3.json` in your Codex folder is **not the same** as the Ruby one. It has 10 rolls and nobody goes bankrupt; the Ruby one has 15 rolls and Sweedal goes bankrupt. If you submit the C# version, make sure your README explains whichever `rolls_3` you actually include.
- Your `Board.cs` prints `Checking space at index ...` lines whenever the board loads. That also breaks `--json` output, because those lines come before the JSON. Remove them before you submit.
